abstract: This learner-driven session covers four common types of uncommon anemia encountered in family medicine, focusing on diagnoses beyond iron deficiency, B12, or folate deficiency. Each group presents a case with history, exam, and lab findings for others to diagnose, followed by a teaching pearl. Topics include anemia of chronic disease, thalassemia, myelodysplastic syndrome, and anemia of chronic kidney disease. The session emphasizes the importance of a thorough history, peripheral smear, and appropriate workup before jumping to treatment, with pearls on avoiding unnecessary iron supplementation and recognizing red flags like hemoglobin below 9 in chronic disease.
key_points: Anemia of chronic disease typically does not drop hemoglobin below 9 g/dL; if lower, consider concomitant iron deficiency or another cause.
In anemia of chronic disease, do not give iron unless there is proven concomitant iron deficiency.
Thalassemia requires hemoglobin electrophoresis to differentiate major/minor and alpha/beta; avoid iron supplementation unless iron deficiency is confirmed.
Myelodysplastic syndrome (MDS) can present with macrocytic anemia and normal B12/folate/TSH; a peripheral smear is essential for diagnosis.
MDS can transform to acute myeloid leukemia (AML), requiring hematology referral.
Anemia of chronic kidney disease (CKD) typically presents with hemoglobin <10 g/dL; consider erythropoietin (EPO) therapy in conjunction with nephrology.
When giving EPO for CKD anemia, iron stores are rapidly depleted, so iron supplementation is often needed even without iron deficiency.
Elevated BUN in CKD shortens RBC lifespan, contributing to anemia beyond erythropoietin deficiency.
For initial anemia workup, obtain a reticulocyte count and direct Coombs test to guide further evaluation.
If MCV is high and B12/folate/TSH are normal, consider MDS or hemolysis; a high reticulocyte count suggests hemolysis.
